en: *Guhyasiddhi* of Padmavajra,
edited by Samdhong Rinpoche and Vajravallabh Dwivedi,
in *Guhyādi-aṣṭasiddhisaṃgraha*.
Sarnath, 1987. (Rare Buddhist Text Series 1).
Typed by Ryugen Tanemura.
The Guhyasiddhi,
composed by the venerable Padmavajrapāda.
First Chapter. Oṃ, homage to Prajñopāya. Homage to Vajratīkṣṇa.

The state of supreme Śiva is free from worldly conventions, all-pervading, devoid of intrinsic nature, eternally arisen, worshipped by the lords of ascetics and the bulls among the best of sages, and beyond the need for meditative concentration. 1.1.
Having prostrated to that reality which is ultimately beyond the reach even of the Buddhas,
[I shall compose this work] according to my own ability upon the glorious body of the Victors— a certain supreme state, pure and sublime.

I shall proclaim the *Śrī-Guhyasiddhi*, most exquisitely composed, auspicious, and like a jewel, for the sake of attaining Buddhahood; it is the foremost messenger in the search for the supreme state,
followed by various masters, the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age, and the dispeller of obstacles and distractions.
The birthplace of all accomplishments, the abode of hundreds of virtues, and the mother of the Victors. || 1.2 ||
-sucaritām] em. ed.; sucaritam MS;
śreyasīm] em. ed.; śreyasī MS;
ratnabhūtām] em. ed.; ratnabhūtā MS
Having first prostrated to Mahāsukha, the support of infinite qualities, whose body is indivisible from the three vajras, and whose sphere transcends the path of speech; (3)
Padmavajra, his mind permeated with compassion, will proclaim the unsurpassed secret accomplishment for the benefit of practitioners. (4)
That which was spoken by the Lord of Beings through many other tantras, and which is endowed with the instruction of a reliable authority, is now being related by me. (5)
Having abandoned the extensive generation stage— the meditation of a beginner— from afar by means of the yoga of the completion stage and with every effort, [verse 6].
Relying upon the *Tantrasadbhāva*, [I shall explain] the characteristics of the collection of attainments and doubts,
having set aside all extensive elaborations that act as obstacles to meditative cultivation.
In brief, I shall describe the divine, auspicious, and unsurpassed secret accomplishment that bestows the siddhi of Buddhahood through the application of wisdom and means. (8)
The source of auspiciousness, effortless, and the destroyer of all obstacles,
she is like another wish-fulfilling gem, a treasury of all spiritual accomplishments.
She is the mother of all Buddhas, the crusher of the enemy of distraction, the accomplisher of all aims, and characterized by perfect enlightenment. || 10 ||
Siddhas arise wherever practitioners may be situated, provided they are endowed with divine means and firmly established in meditative visualizations. || 11 ||
They attain supreme awakening, whose nature is the indivisibility of the three vajras;
yet, under the guise of a secret vow, they are even antagonists of the Dharma. (12)
Those who take life, who are cruel, and who delight in cruel deeds, go to the unsurpassed state, free from the limitations of time.
Even those people who live by deceiving others with the web of false speech,
they too quickly attain success through their practice where it is perfected.
Those who approach the wives of others, those who steal the wealth of others (those who seize the property of others), and even those who constantly perform loathsome deeds; || 15 ||
Having practiced this, practitioners swiftly proceed beyond the desire realm to the higher [realms]; I shall now declare it to you in the form of a secret vow. (16)
By means of this supreme, divine secret conduct, which includes skillful means and bestows all accomplishments, the state of Vajrasattva is attained in this very life. (17)
Those who desire the supreme peace, the eternal state of the Buddhas,
should practice the supreme and auspicious secret accomplishment (*guhyasiddhi*) in order to attain it. (18)
Having meditated through the yoga of the completion stage in conjunction with the principles, otherwise, by those devoid of the principles, no accomplishment whatsoever is attained. (19)
For reality is indeed beyond conceptual construction, devoid of all adjuncts,
signless, appearance-less, free from dualities, and supremely auspicious.
As long as the ritual procedures of the scriptures and traditions are conceptualized through reasoning, they expand extensively, like a drop of oil upon water. (21)

Therefore, enough for now with that [treatise] which produces further conceptualizations, for one who is established in reality and whose form consists of the stage of generation (utpattikrama). || 22 ||

Having first understood reality through its true nature, one performs the ritual for the accomplishment of reality; thereafter, having established the conventional [truth], one proceeds with meditation and so forth according to reality. (23)
Thereafter, one whose mind is illuminated by reality should perform the conduct;
immediately following that, the vow endowed with the Vidyā should indeed be undertaken. (24)
Otherwise, what is the use of a vow for one devoid of reality, which serves merely as a means of livelihood and brings about rebirth in hell? (25)
Practitioners who are devoted to the reality (tattva) attain success even without [observing] vows;
those devoid of reality do not succeed, even through the performance of hundreds of vows.
For practitioners who are united with reality and are entirely stainless, they achieve success through the power of meditation, being liberated from all defilements. (27)
And that reality is clearly established in the *Śrīsamāja* tantra;
elsewhere it is taught secretly through manifold elaborations. (28)
Through the divisions of Kriyā, Caryā, and so forth, and by means of the Sūtrānta-piṭaka and other collections,
that which is one, supreme, and pure is established as not being of a single form. (29)
The Lord of Buddhas, having concealed the reality with great effort according to the varying dispositions of sentient beings, has established it within the jewel-casket of the aggregates. (30)
Having understood that through effort, the supreme and pure *bodhicitta* is firmly established within one's own body by the grace of the Guru's feet. (31)
Then, remaining at home, one should perform the conduct or the meditative cultivation, with a self purified by the jewel of reality and free from all dualities. (32)
Otherwise, those who perform [rites] devoid of divine means, violating the rules of conduct and other precepts, are cooked in the Raurava hell.
Just as when this fire is blazing, a heap of grass, wood, and so forth, once cast into it, turns to ashes and shall never again sprout. (34)
But those who, devoid of reality, perform such extremely marvelous acts, perish and go to hell for as long as space endures. 35.
That divine state, designated as the Reality (tattva), is difficult to attain;
I shall now explain that pure means by which it is attained. (36)
For those who perceive no difference between the Guru and the Vajra-holder, they attain here that reality characterized by the mass of accomplishments (siddhi). || 37 ||

But as for those who are conceited, cruel, deceitful, fraudulent, and deceptive, whose minds are attached to passion and the like—from where could they have obtained it, and from where indeed could they not have obtained it? (38)
But bowing to the guru with deceit, they are intent on searching for his faults;
being wicked and possessed of false pride, they are always delighted in verbal disputes. (39)
Those beings whose minds are bound by the intent to deceive their vajra-brothers and gurus do not attain that supreme state which bestows the highest accomplishment.
Others also are seen here who, having served their gurus with firm devotion through prostrations, worship, and hospitality, have attained whatever they desired. (41)
But when that divine state is attained, even though it stands right before them, those evil-minded ones do not recognize it, wondering, "Who is this, and from where has he come here? (42)
Even when they see him alone from afar, they offer a firm salutation;
yet, when he is among many, there is a lack of even a welcome. (43)
But those beings who are of such a kind do not attain that supreme state, the ultimate nirvana, which was spoken by the Teacher of Reality. 44.
Furthermore, other beings are also seen who revile their teachers, devoid of shame, of wicked conduct, and detractors of genuine virtues. (45)
Merely by collecting tantras, those who are turned away from the nature of reality—neither consecrated nor truly knowledgeable—engage in the gathering of disciples. (46)
Having merely taken up the books themselves and seen them, they are delighted;
yet, being devoid of the conduct of the pledge (samaya), they do not recognize the teacher at all. (47)
And they perform a favor for sentient beings by means of the command of the book, yet they do not understand the reality that was spoken by the Teacher of Truth. 48.
For all these and those who have committed evil deeds and have set out upon the wrong path, there is but one single destination: that of hell.
One who desires the accomplishment of the Sugata’s path must not dwell even for a moment with these difficult-to-restrain individuals who have abandoned the conduct of the sacred pledge. (50)
Having attended upon the teacher for a long time with firm body, speech, and mind, and with his whole being, until he has reached the highest satisfaction. || 51 ||
Then, by the grace of the Guru’s feet, the disciple attains without obstacle the perfectly pure reality established in the oral tradition. (52)
By cultivating this day and night, accomplishment is swiftly attained through this sovereign of principles, which has the nature of the non-duality of the three vajras. (53)
And the accomplishment of the lords of practitioners has been extensively taught in many different tantras through mantras, mudrās, recitation, fire offerings, vows, and so forth. (54)

By means of the fourfold ritual of the twilight prayers (*sandhyā-vidhi*), by the drawing of the mandalas of the regions, and by the conceptualizations of the *kulas* according to the distinctions of color, form, and so forth; || 55 ||

Through bathing, worship, and fasting, as well as by the sequence of binding ritual gestures (mudrā), by the fashioning of images and the like, and through the extensive performance of rites for shrines (caitya). || 56 ||

Thus, although the adepts who speak of reality have described success through millions of conceptual constructions, even by that means they achieve success; however, practitioners do not [truly] exist here.
Therefore, enough of that; for what purpose is it even if it were to exist?
Accomplishment is attained through sufferings exceeding happiness, involving excessive tortures. (58)
But in this [tantra] called the Śrīsamāja, having abandoned all extensive detail, one attains accomplishment in this very life through the yoga of the utpannakrama. || 59 ||
There is nothing superior to the Śrīsamāja as a jewel within the three realms;
it is declared to be the essence of essences among all tantras, each subsequent one being more excellent than the last.
Established through summaries and detailed explanations according to the yoga of the stage of completion (*utpannakrama*),
how can perfect accomplishment (*susiddhi*) be achieved by those who do not know the *Samāja*? (51)
Having abandoned the Śrīsamāja, which cuts through all doubts, removes the darkness of ignorance, and is a jewel-casket for the Buddhas; (62)

The ignorant person desires accomplishments (siddhis) elsewhere that are not conceived through the manifold [realization]; he is like one who strikes at the sky with his fist or attempts to drink from a mirage. 63.
Having abandoned the extensive details of the tantra, one should practice the meditation for beginners, having understood wisdom and means as they truly exist. (64)
Then the wise one, with a single-pointed mind and firm resolve, should practice day and night; having mastered the practice, he attains success—of this there is no doubt. || 65 ||
Neither the lunar day nor the asterism, nor fasting, is prescribed for one endowed with non-dual knowledge; for such a person, the attainment of the Sugata occurs. 66.
Having always cultivated stainless devotion toward Vajradhara, the treasury of virtues— who is the supreme,
singular boat in the ocean of births so deep with the waves of great sins—
the wise person should thereafter commence the practice according to the path taught in the tantras.
It is secret, the source of all virtues, free from impurity, and the bestower of the accomplishment of all aims. || 67 ||

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Reality of the Vow for the Sadhana of Vajrasattva," extracted from the *Śrī Guhyasiddhi*, which is the extraction of the true nature of the tantra of the syllables of ultimate truth.
The Second Chapter.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sādhana arising from the secret.
This is according to the path of the community (samāja), and not by the sequence of other tantras. || 1 ||
Having abandoned the entire path of the outer tantras and kriyā at a great distance, it is explained as it truly is through the yoga of the sequence of the *sāmnāya*. (2)
Many teachers have declared that in the Tantra,
the compiler is the heroic leader Lokeśa, possessed of great splendor in the Śrīsamāja.
We, however, say only this: by the grace of the Guru's feet, there is no other compiler of the *Śrīsamāja*. (4)
The creator of the tantra is the Heart-Vajra; he alone is the speaker and the teacher.
There is no other [teacher] whatsoever, with the exception of Mahāsukha.
Thus, the statement "having heard" which is established in the state of abiding was itself spoken by the Mind-Vajra among all the Buddhas.
Just as the divine [teaching] was spoken by the one known as Śrī Mahāsukha, who abides in the state of *vihāra*, so do I speak something [of it]. (7)
In one supreme location, the Lord himself taught the true essence of the tantras of the Buddhas, which is great bliss. (8)
Having heard that true essence of the Tantra, all the sons of the Victorious Ones trembled, were overcome with terror, and spoke to the Supreme Lord: || 9 ||
[Ed. p.
13] O Lord, why has this nature of phenomena (dharmatā) been so poorly explained?
It generates extreme terror in every respect, even for the Buddhas. (10)
O Lord, you have revealed the unsurpassed Vajrayāna, which was utterly concealed, and have spoken of the equality and oneness of all phenomena. (11)
Speaking thus, those [beings] of great majesty belonging to all the Buddhas,
having caused [the world] to tremble and fallen into a swoon, fixed their minds upon the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
Oh, how marvelous is the teaching of the Vajrayāna, so well-guarded and supremely secret!
It is of a pure nature devoid of intrinsic existence, for which no analogy exists. (13)
Seeing all those Buddhas rendered unconscious, Vajrasattva, relying upon a divine meditative absorption whose nature is the bliss of great bliss, [acted]. 14.
Then, having joined the Buddhas through the application of the vajra and lotus, he spoke sweet words in the form of supreme bliss. (15)
O all you Victors, behold the unfolding of the thought of awakening!
Where there is neither body, nor speech, nor mind, there form is clearly perceived. (16)

As long as one exerts effort through the application of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one reaches the syllable of the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*), which is peaceful, the abode of all Buddhas, and auspicious. (17)
All this is a manifestation of the very nature of wisdom—of that which is free from conceptual proliferation, pure, and divine knowledge in every respect. (18)
That which is supreme, auspicious, and pure, honored by all Buddhas, the ineffable and omnipresent state—this is the miraculous manifestation of the mind. || 19 ||
Thus established, that divine and stainless [reality] is called the sphere of space (khadhātu);
in the form of supreme bliss, it is the source of happiness for all sentient beings. (20)
[Ed. p.
14] Born from the body of wisdom, pure, the abode of all Buddhas, and auspicious—consisting of that, I have served the Buddhas, the imperishable arising of the divine Dharma. (21)
That which is divine, shaped like the letter E, adorned in its center with the syllable Vaṃ, is the abode of all happiness, a jewel-casket for the Buddhas. (22)
Therefore, I shall explain that which is established at the beginning of the tantra;
thus the heroes of great bliss spoke to all the Tathāgatas. (23)
She who indeed, through the union of the body, speech, and mind of all the Buddhas, abides as the bestower of accomplishment, divine and renowned by the name Prajñā. (24)
That which is established within that [lotus] is the pair of syllables *bhagaṃ*;
consisting of that, what is called the pure reality (*śuddhatattva*) has been served by me in the ultimate sense. (25)
Together with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who are the Vajras of the three bodies,
I am established there in that pure realm and dwell according to my will.
There is no other pure state of phenomena apart from the syllable of the source of phenomena (dharmodayākṣara), wherein the Buddhas have arisen and are established in the awakening of a Buddha. (27)

In that regard, do not feel fear concerning the pure reality, which is without abode, the syllable of the source of phenomena (dharmodayā), and the peaceful; for they are established within the Vajra Consort. (28)
From that, the entire world—including animals and all other beings—has arisen.
Why then, O Victors, have you once again fallen into fear? (29)
This supreme nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is the essence produced by the Buddhas;
for those whose sole consummation is the knowledge of that essence, it has not occurred in the past, nor will it ever cease to be.
And having heard those words, all those established in the enlightenment of a Buddha, numbering in the tens of millions, began to offer praise with their bodies bowed low. (31)
And he spoke these sweet words, which desire the welfare of all beings: "O Lord of the World, O Great Hero, O Great Sage, teach the reality! (32)
Completely purified as the foremost of all Buddhas, you set the Vajrayāna in motion; O changeless and non-manifesting one, teach the reality that is without abode. (33)
Just as the Victors have crossed the shoreless ocean of great afflictions, please speak that supreme reality, the most excellent among all realities. (34)
The station of abiding is adorned with such words from the very beginning;
by the mere knowledge of which, the accomplishment of the Sugata is attained. (35)
Having heard this request from the glorious Mahāsukha-vajrin, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak the supreme state. (36)
Just as it was taught by the Mind-Vajra-holder for all the Buddhas, having opened up the ultimate secret, this Compendium of the Essence of the Vajra. (37)
Therefore, having understood everything clearly through the grace of the Guru's feet, I shall proclaim it exactly as it is established. (38)
Therefore, that divine [teaching], which is the collection of all accomplishments (siddhi), is now being told;
it is declared to be the most essential of essences, established at the beginning of the Tantra. (39)
That secret reality which was proclaimed by the Lord of Great Bliss, which gives rise to the happiness of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all sentient beings. (40)
Thus established is the pure syllable "Evam," honored by the three realms, belonging to the Śrī-samāja, the sole king of secret rituals. (41)
That mudrā of the Lord of Beings, which is supremely eternal, is renowned by the name Prajñā; she is pure in the beginning, middle, and end. (42)
Abiding in the form of conventional reality, she arises from the three vajra-knowledges;
she is renowned as the *karmamudrā* for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. (43)
Having assumed a human form, she desires the welfare of all sentient beings;
she is indeed the unsurpassed Goddess Prajñā, pure, omnipresent, and all-pervading. 44.

In the delightful realm of the space-element, the Lord of Beings, compassionate toward the maintenance of the universe, has properly resorted to this single [deity] which brings about the arising of auspiciousness. (45)
Therefore, that which is called "bhaga" consists of these two syllables, *e* and *vam*;
it abides as the union of the body, speech, and mind of all Buddhas. (46)

Therefore, all of this, established through both brief enumeration and detailed exposition, is now set forth with reference to the true essence of the internal (*adhyātmika*) tantra—the most secret of secrets and the ultimate reality—residing within the venerable *Samāja*, the Sun among Tantras.

That is to say, having become the Mind-Vajra— whose form resembles an illusion through the knowledge of the suchness (*tathatā*) of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, both stable and moving, and whose body is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man— the inconceivable ultimate reality (*paramārtha-tattva*) beginning with "Thus" (*evam*) and so forth was taught in the *Śrī-samāja* to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in its ultimate form.
That ultimate reality, the form of the inconceivable deity, which is perfected according to the sequence of the Tantra through the succession of the seventeen Bodhisattvas, shall now be explained.

First, at the conclusion of the enumeration of the names of the seventeen bodhisattvas in the introductory chapter (upoddhātapaṭala), it is stated with reference to that [subject] by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmadhātusvabhāvavibhāvanāvajra:
"This, first of all, is the deity yoga."

Having become one whose nature is the *dharmadhātu* and who possesses the form of being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), consisting of body, speech, and mind, she is established in the space-element together with the four human families of earth and so forth according to the previous [method] through the performance of the rules for the ritual of the pledge (*samaya*), meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and recitation (*jāpa*). By means of the enjoyment of the five qualities of sensory pleasure, she is—inexpressible and beyond expression—the mantra-form presiding over the entire succession of beings, including animals and others, in the form of supreme bliss, the sovereign of supreme happiness, and the presiding deity of the glorious lotus-mandala.

(—jp.17) For the sake of reviving those who have fainted upon hearing the resonance of the reality of the ultimate nature (*paramārthadharmatā*) and the essence of the commitment (*samayatattva*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, that ultimate reality which has been taught as "Thus" (*evam*) and so forth is here declared:
"Therefore, that which is established as secret at the beginning of the Tantra is spoken:
'Thus' (*evam*) is the pure syllable, born from the Vajra Lady. (47)
Thus, what is called the "space-element" is renowned as the "pledge-seal" (samayamudrā);
for it is said that its supreme service consists in hearing [the teachings] within this context. 48.
That which is the condensed, non-conceptual, omniscient gnosis, which is the form of all the *bhaga*s—that is known as the *khadhātu* (the space-element). 49.
That which was stated as "in one" is the subject of description; that has been practiced by me: therein, in what is called the sphere of space, is the ocean of bliss. (50)
In this divine place, most highly honored by all the Buddhas, which is adorned with various bells, garlands, and precious jewels; (51)
The Blessed One is designated as the sovereign lord of the mind;
the Vajra Lady is known as Wisdom, who is the very essence of all Victors. 52.
By the word "all," the Tathāgatas such as Akṣobhya and others are meant;
those who abide therein are their body, speech, and mind. (53)
In the pure bhaga of the Vajra Lady, the Great Hero dwelt in victory through the nature of all phenomena, in the play of supreme bliss. (54)
That divine form shaped like the letter *E*, adorned in its center with the syllable *Vaṃ*, is the supreme abode of the Vajrin, auspicious and born from the body of Prajñā. (55)
There, Buddhas have arisen and in that very place they have attained final nirvana;
throughout infinite millions of eons, as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru. (56)
Then the glorious one dwelt together with the Vajra of Great Bliss, with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, in the glorious Padma-maṇḍala.

That which is called the *khadhātu* (space-element) is seen on all sides like a sesame pod, completely filled with Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. (58) pāda b: -vajriṇā] em. ed.; -vajriṇaḥ MSS.
Having performed the service of that very reality of the syllable through skillful means,
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attain the supreme state. (59)
For the state of abiding is thus established from the perspective of ultimate reality;
otherwise, true realization does not arise for those yogins who seek the truth.
Or else, the glorious King Mahāsukha, who is the Cittavajra and another [as well], is the agent here in this work called the *Samāja*; by him this was well-established. (61)
The two syllables "śru-tam," which are completely pure in this manner and so forth, must be stated with certainty there at the beginning, situated in the secret word. (62)
By this [argument] which is about to be stated, its agency is not accepted;
nor is the elision of the two internal [factors] admitted here in the Tantras and other works. (63)
Having thus known the perfectly pure state, supremely stainless, which is described in the *Śrīsamāja* as the auspicious abode of all Buddhas—[pāda d: *luptiḥ*, em. ed.; *luptim*, MSS]—64.
When that is known, the supreme accomplishment is attained; this is remembered as the pervasion of the Tantra.
It is said to be like a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), showing the conduct of the observances (samaya). 65.
In truth, within that pure and ineffable bodhicitta, the Guide of the Path abides, having entered into it in its full extent. (66)
That which is established as inexpressible within the peaceful *dharmodayā* exists pervading the universe through its infinite manifestations. (67)
Having completely abandoned all those distinctions like leaves and husks,
I shall proclaim the means for realizing that which is of pure nature. (68)

That reality which is devoid of intrinsic nature, born from the lotus and the vajra, together with its means—that which is established as the objective at the conclusion of the joys of cessation (viramānanda)—is that very thing. (69)
By this, practitioners established in the tantras—who are constantly intent in mind, devoted to meditative cultivation, and awakened by divine knowledge—attain accomplishment. (70)
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Cessation of the State of Abiding," in the *Śrī Guhyasiddhi*, extracted from the essence of the tantra of the syllables of ultimate truth.
The third chapter: Therefore, that secret cultivation of wisdom and means is now being told.
The recollection of the Mind-Vajra is the supreme [practice], more secret than the secret. (1)
I shall correctly explain for those who do not know that purity which is established even within their own bodies, so that they may accomplish the divine state. (2)
In accordance with the path of the *Śrīsamāja*, for the sake of attaining the renowned divine accomplishments (*divyasiddhi*),
[I shall explain] how it is correctly established within the divine abode of the *khadhātu*. (3)
It generates consciousness, is divine, and is pure in its beginning, middle, and end;
it is the objective for beginner practitioners and acts as a means of producing conviction.
From the union of the vajra and the element of space, and from their contact, a most wonderful bliss arises; that which produces supreme bliss. (5)
From the exhaustion of that [thought], there is cessation; and that cessation which is supreme, whose nature is indefinable, something indeed arises.
Free from all sense faculties, beyond dualities, supremely auspicious, all-pervading, and devoid of intrinsic nature—that is enlightenment, the supreme state. (7)
The divine [state] called Samantabhadra, situated at the end of the Cessation (virama), is indeed proclaimed as the supreme place of liberation for practitioners. || 8 ||
As it was said by the Tathāgatas in the Śrīsamāja:
"The supreme, utterly pure, unsurpassed bodhicitta is devoid of intrinsic nature. (9)
I shall now explain the description of that pure nature:
one should meditate upon a moon mandala situated in the center of the space element.
And so forth is said:
that which is situated above the space-element (*khadhātu*) like a jewel, having the nature of all bliss.
In the center, that which serves as the sign adorned with qualities is said to be at the tip of the "man's nose" in this [treatise]. || 11 ||
But upon that [wind], one should meditate on the mind known as conceptual, in the form of the moon, the image of the Buddha;
that which has the nature of the bliss of the enjoyment body (sāmbhogikakāya) is called the conventional bodhicitta. || 12 ||

The conventional bodhicitta has set; there, it is accompanied by many various Buddhas who have arisen with the perception of detachment, manifesting through diverse, quivering, and incomparable emanation bodies. || 13 ||
That state which is designated as cessation, arising from moments and so forth, existing among mobile beings, established and named after a mustard seed—that, the Buddhas call the Nirmāṇakāya. (14)

When the emanation body has been attained and entered here into the enjoyment body, which is of the nature of bliss, the vajra of selflessness—having shaken off the web of conceptual constructions and discursive thoughts—is realized according to the ritual procedure and in due order. (15)
But your hands, through that utterly stainless Vajra of Selflessness, were instantly made one with the state of Awakening, like clarified butter poured into clarified butter. (16)
Having attained the bliss of cessation there, they have entered the very firm vajra of selflessness;
that which abides there, known as the unobstructed, is the all-pervading, pure state of awakening. (17)
By that very means, one should meditate upon the divine, infinite-splendored universe, which consists of the object of knowledge;
that which is the ultimate limit of cessation, to be accomplished through the focal point, and whose form is inconceivable. (18)

Having understood, according to the prescribed method, that the body of the Victors— which is pure in the ultimate sense— is like a stainless wish-fulfilling gem called the "Auspicious Vase," which is devoid of intrinsic nature on all sides and is to be personally realized within oneself, [one perceives] its splendor. (19)

Then, having diligently released the body and the senses from the flickering rays of a single mirage and the like, I shall describe according to the rule the nature of existence—the one that appears in manifold forms within the three realms. (20)
Having learned through the grace of the Guru's feet how that reality, which is without means, is to be grasped with effort, the wise one should meditate upon it. (21)

One should meditate upon oneself as pure and peaceful, united with that reality; whether through the action-seal (karmamudrā) or otherwise, one will attain accomplishment—of this there is no doubt. || 22 ||
This meditation, which is accompanied by the action seal (karmamudrā) through the union of the vajra and the lotus, has been taught as it truly is by the Speaker of Reality. 23.
For the sake of revealing the spirit of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) to beginner beings, one must rely on the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), since the objective cannot be attained elsewhere. (24)

Otherwise, for those engaged in the initial practice, there is no conventional reality within the three realms; [only] when that divine state is honored, which is stainless in its beginning, middle, and end. (25) pāda c: *karmamudrāṃ* em. ed.; *karmamudrā* MSS.
This supreme reality, peaceful and established as that which is called the space-element (khadhātu), is obtained through the union of the vajra and the lotus and from the oral tradition. (26)
Even though it is omnipresent, its apprehension by beginners occurs in the divine abode of the space-element; it is attained there by the most excellent practitioners. (27)
That which is supreme nirvāṇa, whose nature is bliss and is formless—that is the Mudrā, relying upon which conventional reality exists. (28)

Having thus understood through reality the cultivation of wisdom and means, [one sees that they] are established as they truly are within the peaceful syllable of the source of phenomena (dharmodayā), by way of its conventional form. (29)
Then one should perform the most wonderful sādhana of the Wielder of the Vajra, joined with the means of one's own body, or else through the action-seal (karmamudrā). 30.
[The reading *pramādbhutam* is adopted as the emendation by the editor; the manuscripts read *paramādbhutaḥ*.
Seated upon a lotus, established in a manner distinct from the *karmamudrā*, the tranquil Śrīvajrin is the object of focus through successive stages of meditative cultivation. (31)
All that has been told by me, and I shall speak further:
for those endowed with reality, meditation is devoid of the action-seal (karmamudrā).
I shall now briefly explain how a practitioner attains the divine state of supreme nirvāṇa even without the mudrā. (33)
Having abandoned the deceptive and cruel action-seal (karmamudrā) as well as the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā),
which abounds in conceptual construction, one should meditate upon the great seal (mahāmudrā).
Having abandoned the human seal (mudrā) which gives rise to all distractions, one should practice the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) conjoined with the means (upāya) of one's own body. 35.
For that supreme and auspicious Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) is self-cognizable knowledge;
though it resides within the support of one's own body, it is not perceived by those of meager wisdom. (36)
By means of the supreme [knowledge] alone, that which is subject to transformation within one's own body is known exactly as it exists, through the grace of the Guru’s command. (37)
Having understood thus, one should with effort [meditate upon] the auspicious Prajñāpāramitā, the all-pervading Supreme Goddess, by means of the yoga of the utpannakrama. 38.
Then one should perform the practice that is desired and prompted by the heart, which, through the application of skillful means, bestows the accomplishment of Buddhahood. (39)
The knower of reality should always contemplate himself as having become one with her, day and night; he attains success, there is no doubt in this. || 40 ||
Henceforth, I shall explain the practice that grants all accomplishments, and how the secret is situated within the body composed of the five aggregates. (41)
I shall explain the well-guarded conceptualization of Mahāmudrā, just as it is accomplished by the heroes within their own supreme bodies. (42)
The wise person should not cultivate existence, and should abandon non-existence from afar. (pāda c: *nirvartyate*, emended by the editor; *nirvartate*, MSS)
In one [of the two] permanence is to be grasped; in the other also, emptiness. (43)
Through the conjunction of permanence and annihilation, when ultimate reality is realized, there arises a certain non-dual gnosis, pure in its beginning, middle, and end. (44)
Eternal, all-pervading, supreme, and profoundly peaceful; devoid of causes and examples;
liberated from both existence and non-existence; ever-arisen and undisturbed. (45)
Non-abiding nirvana, in which all defilements have been shaken off, is beyond the range even of the Buddhas who are endowed with the absence of intrinsic nature. 46.
pāda b: [vidhūta-] nidhūta- MS ga:
There is no goer to be found there, nor is going sought anywhere at all; from the perspective of ultimate reality, neither the meditator, the meditation, nor the object of meditation exists. (47)
Inexpressible and indefinable, devoid of the grasped and the grasper, without characteristics and stainless—that is proclaimed as Nirvāṇa. (48)
That which is declared supreme, designated as Mahāmudrā, the divine state of both saṃsāra and liberation, is the supreme state known as Nirvāṇa. || 49 ||
That divine state of sentient beings is firm according to their capacity; though it is truly one, it appears as two through the power of their respective dispositions. 50.
Divine, in the form of nirvāṇa, pure and naturally stainless, it is established everywhere in the forms of women, men, and so forth. || 51 ||
That is beyond the senses, peaceful, ineffable, all-pervading, supreme, free from decay and destruction, and designated as the glorious Great Bliss (Śrīmahāsukha). 52.
In that delightful state of the three realms, everything whatsoever that is designated as a substance has arisen and is situated everywhere. (53) [a: *tad atīndriyaṃ* em. ed.; *yat tadīndriyaṃ* MSS]
That is the seed of all things and the supreme state of all accomplishments;
it is the ultimate abode of the Buddhas, known by the name Sukhāvatī. (54)
From that [source], all gods, Daityas, and humans have emerged;
the entire triple world (traidhātuka) without exception is established therein. 55.
That whose form is not known, which is devoid of speech and intellect, which transcends sound, smell, and taste, and which is beyond the range of the mind; || 56 ||
For him who has transcended the world and its origins, whose supreme form is wondrous, and who acts with complete independence, the Wheel of Dharma is set in motion. (57)
From that [source], all the countless millions of Manus have emerged, as well as whatever authoritative scriptures there are that teach the sequence of reality. (58)
Having thus understood the reality through the grace of the Guru's feet, by whatever means that supreme form—which has come from the Inexpressible—is attained. (59)
Then the wise mantra-practitioner should truly perfect his own body by adopting a posture that is properly joined and infused with the state of non-existence (abhāva).
Endowed with divine means and having repeatedly exerted effort,
one who is completely liberated from all dualities will certainly be pierced before long. (61)
But he who, having understood her well-guarded tradition through this [teaching], is pure in soul and endowed with the five qualities of sensual pleasure, should meditate [upon her]. (62)
Established in the secret accomplishment, he succeeds without a doubt—whether joined with the action-seal (karmamudrā) or endowed with the great seal (mahāmudrā). 63.
This supreme nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is born from the essence of the Buddhas;
for those whose sole faculty is the knowledge of that essence, it has neither been nor will it ever be otherwise.
There is no other pure bestower of accomplishment than this selfless state, which is free from conceptual construction and without support—the place from which the Buddhas have arisen. (65)
This supreme goddess Prajñā is indeed declared to be unsurpassed;
she bestows liberation upon all sentient beings, provided she is known and meditated upon. (66)
But he who is pure in soul should meditate, according to the sequence of the previously taught ritual, upon the self that is naturally luminous, pure, and born from all vajras. (67)
Having abandoned the ordinary body, with a mind that has attained divine power, [he beholds the Buddha] endowed with the excellence of all aspects and adorned with all the primary marks. (68)
Endowed with skillful means and established in the true samādhi, he succeeds through the miraculous transformations of the lotus and vajra; of this there is no doubt.
That great bliss which is attained when conjoined with Mahāmudrā is the supreme, divine nectar of gnosis; it cannot indeed be described in words. (70)
That reality is to be personally realized; it cannot be expressed in words.
It is accessible through the cultivation of devotion, but otherwise it is not accessible at all. 71.
Having realized the truth and then cultivated a state of devotion day and night, [one should act].
In that state of supreme nirvana, which is peaceful and unsurpassed. || 72 ||
Then, through the power of devotion, there arises within that [state] a certain supreme form produced by the force of meditative cultivation, born of bliss. (73)
Arising with the form of the syllable *dhag*, it performs the process of emanation and reabsorption, illuminating all this— *bhūr*, *bhuvar*, and *svar*— along with everything moving and unmoving.
By the power of the reality of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanātattvasāmarthyāt*), Śiva— consisting of wisdom and means (*prajñopāyātmaka*),
liberated from all afflictions (*sarvakleśavinirmukta*), and adorned with all auspicious marks (*sarvalakṣaṇabhūṣita*)— [arises]. (75)
The supreme state, born from the knowledge of emptiness, is free from duality;
it is endowed with the excellence of all aspects and devoid of the grasped and the grasper. || 76 ||
Knowledge is like an illusion—pure, clear, and naturally stainless;
it transcends sound, smell, and taste, and is devoid of form and touch. || 77 ||
Only by means of the single eye of knowledge within meditative absorption is seen that divine state, which is like a shadow or an illusion and is associated with all of saṃsāra. (78)
Those who contemplate reality attain a body resembling a rainbow, composed of various and manifold forms, and radiant with garlands of the blazing fire of wisdom. (79)
Through the power of the application of meditation and by the observance of the commitments,
such a form is attained that cannot even be described by the Victors.
Where there is neither body, nor speech, nor mind, that supreme state which is all-pervading—
therein the form of him who is realized is manifested through the power of the oral tradition.
Oh, how truly marvelous! Oh, how peaceful and beyond the reach of the senses!
Oh, how supremely profound is this miraculous manifestation of the mind of awakening! (82)
Having attained such a sequence, this unsurpassed yoga of the deity, one should then perform the conduct for the sake of accomplishing the state of Buddhahood. (83)
The locus of all afflictions is the state devoid of the signified and the signifier;
having examined this with effort again and again, the practitioner [should proceed]. (84)
One should practice the secret conduct with a firm mind and absolute certainty, free from all dualities through the yoga of the completion stage. 85.
Just as no fatigue arises through divine acts such as laughter and dance, the practitioner,
observing the vow, should practice the secret vow with resolute conviction in the state of a Buddha. 86.
Abiding in that divine vow which cuts through all afflictions,
one who is endowed with the realization of the lack of intrinsic nature should accomplish the supreme state.
That supreme secret which is established in the tantra and in the mouth of the guru—
divine, bestowing both wisdom and supernatural powers— all of that has been told by me. (88)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Instruction on Perfect Enlightenment," in the *Śrīguhyasiddhi*, extracted from the *Paramārthasatyākṣaratantrasadbhāva*.
[Ed. p. 28] The Fourth Chapter.
Therefore, I shall now explain something else in some detail:
the cultivation of the generation stage for beginner beings. (1)
As it was clearly stated by the Lord of Beings in the *Śrīsamāja*:
"The fourfold [stages] of meditation are [attained] by means of the progressively higher paths. (2)

First is the placement of the syllables (akṣaranyāsa), established according to the order of generation (utpattikrama); second is the meditation (bhāvanā) for the best of practitioners according to its own essential nature.
The third is the supreme, divine cultivation of the *jñānamudrā*;
the fourth is declared to be the superior cultivation of the *mahāmudrā*.
This fourfold set has been correctly established according to reality; I shall now explain individually that cultivation which has been taught by me. (5)
That meditation which has been described by means of the arrangement of syllables is said to be for the purpose of introducing beginner practitioners.
First, it is explained exactly as it is established:
according to the yoga of the generation stage (utpattikrama), each single [deity] is fivefold.
I shall here explain that supreme purity which is established through the wisdom of the fivefold manifest enlightenment, so that it may be firmly understood.
As it was said by Cittavajra: "Through the yoga of the successive placement of syllables, I am indeed the nature of the *dharmadhātu* in progressive order. (9)
Divine, characterized by space, and free from all conceptual constructions,
knowledge is perfectly pure everywhere, stainless in its beginning, middle, and end.
In which the intrinsic natures of phenomena are established as having distinct forms,
they are scrutinized through effort by means of the supreme yoga of selflessness. (11)
That form which is liberated from all conceptual proliferation and is the supreme Śiva, known as the very nature of the dharmadhātu—that is proclaimed here as gnosis (jñāna). || 12 ||
Abiding in that divine state, which is free from all afflictions,
that supreme form is taken as the object for the sake of performing the welfare of sentient beings.
Endowed with divine means, his form is produced by wisdom;
he arises instantaneously in appearance, adorned with all the primary marks.
Complete with all ornaments, ungraspable, supremely auspicious, transparent, undisturbed, pure, and awakened through Mahāmudrā. (15)
Therefore, that which is produced from form, which imitates its shadow, which resembles an illusion, divine, and mental in nature—this is the form of the mudrā. (16)
That wisdom which arises from infinite qualities and is unknowable even to the Buddhas is here called the "Glorious Mirror. (17)
That knowledge in which whatever is investigated is seen through logical reasoning to have the nature of being without intrinsic existence—that is called the knowledge of equality. (18)
Having expanded the divine Śrī-padma-maṇḍala within the discourse known as the *Vacanā*, one should carefully contemplate the supreme state of all the Tathāgatas. (19)
Having expanded [it], and having examined it by means of the state of selflessness, [one perceives it] as having the nature of being devoid of intrinsic existence.
The divine realm of the element of space, the supreme abode of all Buddhas.
As long as it is not examined through the application of subtle analysis, so long does something appear therein; and what is it that has been impelled? 21.
Whatever Buddhas and Bodhisattvas there may be dwelling within the abode of the three realms of existence, they are seen there on all sides like sesame seeds in a pod. (4.22)
Having thus beheld that divine multitude of Buddhas of great splendor,
one should practice this yoga in the divine abode of the expanse of space.
In this [place],
all the Tathāgatas— those who exist now, those from the past, and those others who will exist in the future— have this supreme station. (4.24)
That which is pure and unclouded is all endowed with the state of a Tathāgata;
in brief, it is called gnosis, and that is what is being examined. (4.25)
Having carefully examined everything that is supreme and pertaining to the Tathāgatas, one should thereafter perform the miraculous manifestation of the vajra-lotus. (4.26)
Having ascended to the yoga of the deity by way of the nature of supreme bliss,
and having relied upon the bodhicitta, one proceeds through the sequence of earth and the other elements.
Having relied upon [the elements],
having produced the form of the deity in the sequence beginning with earth, that which is desired shines forth therein.
That which is established by the families of Śāśvata, Akṣobhya, Ratna, Āya, and the rest. || 4.28 ||

...Akṣobhya...; by means of the yoga of the universal monarch (*cakravartin*) and so forth, there is the cultivation of the Knowledge-Person (*vidyāpuruṣa*), endowed with divine ornaments and awakened through the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). (4.29)
United with the vajra and lotus, having the nature of supreme bliss,
he manifests in various and manifold forms through the radiating waves of gnosis.
The knowledge of the performance of duties is said to be that supreme, stainless state, wherein the seals (mudrās) of the Victors abide and from which their manifestation arises. (4.31)
That which is endowed with these five equal states is here proclaimed as the wisdom of the fivefold manifest enlightenment. (4.32)

That which is established in the stage of the generation process (utpattikrama) is explained in its specific details, exactly as it is systematically arranged through the yoga of deity meditation (devatābhāsa). 4.33
[It is] established as such,
endowed with the six elements and the wheel-turning kings mentioned in the Tantra, together with the four primary families and the wrathful beings equal to them. (4.34)
Endowed with the sixteen Bodhisattvas and their retinues, as well as the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor characteristics. || 4.35 ||
This fivefold perfect awakening has been proclaimed by the Tathāgatas; it is established through the families of Śāśvata, Akṣobhya, Ratna, Āya, and the others, along with the secondary marks. (4.36)
Having thus conceptualized [it] through various forms, it is encompassed by the *samaya*.
That is declared to be the meditation for beginner beings. (4.37)
This is declared to be the external cultivation of the sequence of the beings,
which was first established through the yoga of the placement of syllables. (4.38)
For beginner beings, there is another, higher, and supreme meditation on the action-seal (karmamudrā), which is established as residing within a lotus. (4.39)
Furthermore, having meditated upon the locus of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhānapada*), one should then perform the worship.
For this is the supreme secret even for the Vajra-holders in the *Śrīsamāja*. (4.40)
Through the union of the vajra and the lotus, endowed with the arising from one's own kalpa—this is indeed the second meditation, proclaimed as the "essential nature" (svarūpa). (4.41)
The third stage prescribed for him is the cultivation of the internal state,
which consists of the conceptualization of the Wisdom-Seal (jñānamudrā) endowed with the excellence of all aspects.
And the fourth [chapter] in the *Uttara-tantra* is that which brings about perfect awakening;
beyond which there exists no other cultivation of Mahāmudrā. (4.43)
[The editor's emendation *cottare* for *cottaraṃ* in the manuscript (MS) at p. 32:
It is liberated from all sense faculties and protected by the speaker of reality.
It bestows swift accomplishment, is peaceful, and is established within the mouth of the Guru.
It bestows accomplishment;
it is neither one nor many, and it is not both one and many. It is waveless, without appearance, and established facing every direction. (4.45)
Established as that which is to be known through mere conventional reality, it brings about supreme bliss;
it is the massing away of the flood of afflictions, the embodiment of true wisdom. (4.46)
Having thus understood the supreme yoga of the deity within the sequence of the tantra, that which has been arrived at by this method through the successive stages of the path— || 4.47 ||
Then, having gradually abandoned all meditative objects, the mantra-practitioner should constantly and with great effort cultivate Mahāmudrā. (4.48)
Endowed with skillful means, divine, bestowing all accomplishments, and auspicious—
one who is joined with the contemplation focused upon that attains perfection in this very birth.
The mind's state of realizing non-arising is the Unsurpassed;
its lack of intrinsic nature is wisdom, while skillful means is said to be present therein. (4.50)
Having thus understood the visualization of Mahāmudrā according to reality, one should then perform the practice together with its means, whichever vow is desired and pleasing. (4.51)
Whether it be Buddhist, or Jain, or Śaiva, or Pāśupata; or else the divine Great Vow, or whatever else is pleasing to the mind. (4.52)
In that regard, the wise have declared that the practice prescribed by the Arhatas should be known as constant; whatever is conducive to the mind should be performed without hesitation. (4.53)

Having understood with effort the entire incomparable path as it is threaded through the glorious *Samāja*, the one of pure and firm intellect, having abandoned everything external, remains solely intent upon the pure reality. (4.54)

Having abandoned all attachment, one should meditate day after day and without ceasing upon the one who possesses a stainless natural body and is endowed with divine bliss, who is permeated by the illusion of primordial wisdom (*jñāna-māyā*), for the sake of attaining Buddhahood.

Endowed with divine bliss, their hearts overflowing with joy, they have fixed their minds upon awakening; constantly permeated by meditative cultivation, all their impurities destroyed, and the bonds of saṃsāra cast off. (4.55)

With a one-pointed mind, the yogi of reality, whose veil of impurity has been removed and who is purified by divine vision, should meditate upon himself through the application of the placement of the true steps that lead to the state of supreme bliss.
The chapter on the removal of impurities is concluded.
In a secluded place, in a secret location, on a mountain that is the abode of hundreds of virtues,
in an empty house, in a ruined garden, in a cave, in the abode of the ancestors, or in a delightful underground chamber— || 4.56 ||
In these locations and regions, one whose resolve is purified by these practices and who possesses the divine marks should,
free from attachment, meditate upon the Vajrī— the jewel of reality— who bestows the bliss of the sense objects.
This is for all yogins who are devoted to the path of reality.
Their success comes through the application of skillful means and reasoning, and not otherwise. 4.57
Through the yoga of the generation stage, it may also be otherwise;
however, it is proclaimed that in this [system], accomplishment is not attained within a single lifetime. (4.58)
Having thus known with certainty the cultivation of wisdom and means, one should abandon the distinctions of ritual action and all external forms without exception. (4.59)
Following the path of the *Śrī-samāja*, the wise one should practice the secret accomplishment (*guhyasiddhi*) which bestows the attainment of Buddhahood, endowed with divine means. 4.60
Place, time, lunar day, day of the week, and constellation constitute the external mandala.
Without these, I shall explain the sādhana of the Holder of the Vajra. (4.61)

The practice that brings about Buddhahood, which was taught by the Supreme among Bipeds according to the prescribed ritual, and which consists of many various and beautiful conducts, is clearly set forth in the *Samāja Tantra*. (4.62) [vajradhāriṇaḥ em. ed.; vajradhāriṇam MS]
There is no accomplishment without her, as long as she has not been cultivated;
having understood this, let those skilled in discernment undertake the practice according to rule,
which brings about the perfection of Buddhahood.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Complete Enlightenment in Five Aspects," in the *Śrīguhyasiddhi*, extracted from the *Śrīparamārthasattryakṣarasadbhāva*.
[Ed. p. 34] The Fifth Chapter.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the secret *sādhana* of Vajrasattva, the secret of the illustrious Guhyavajrin, which has been concealed by his conduct in accordance with reality.
Through the yoga of the generation stage, there is the destruction of the enemy that is distraction;
it is easily accomplished, auspicious, secret, and a means for accomplishing the activity of play. || 5.2 ||
This supreme, divine [tantra], accompanied by consecration, is realized through the Śrīsamāja;
in it, practitioners who are established in secret siddhi attain accomplishment. (5.3)
Having practiced through divine knowledge, free from all mental forms,
and liberated from all dualities, they remain established wherever they may be.
I shall explain with effort that supreme state of the siddhis—
the secret accomplishment— in brief, for the benefit of practitioners.
Whoever desires to attain perfection in this very life must observe the secret vow, which destroys all dualities. (5.6)
In the empowerment known as the *Samāja*, which is the source of all bliss, she bestows divine accomplishment through the empowerment of Mahāmudrā. (5.7)

Then, having established himself in self-will and being solely intent upon the primordial yoga, he [attained] the jewel of the yoga of practice which has issued forth from the mouth of the Guru. (5.8)
Therefore, I shall fully explain that consecration which is well-guarded, the supreme [teaching] more secret than the secret, protected by the Lord of Great Bliss. 5.9
Having diligently obtained a beautiful consort who gives rise to virtuous qualities, one should offer her to the Ācārya, who is knowledgeable in the rules and conduct of the Tantra. 5.10.
With offerings of milk and lamps, and with extensive arrays of perfumes and garlands—em. ed.; jñāmā MS [ed. p. 35].
Having performed worship, the wise one should worship the Vajra-holder together with the mudrā.

Having worshipped and praised him according to the prescribed rite, the wise one should, with devotion, honor the Guru in a secluded place along with the ritual hand-gestures (mudrās), following the sequence of procedures declared in the Kalpa.
Having placed his right knee upon the ground,
he should entreat the Wielder of the Thunderbolt according to the ritual with this King of Hymns.
O Omniscient One, Lord of all stages, Sovereign of all, Master of the world! O Great Hero, Lord of heroes, homage be to you! 5.14
Abiding as the self-nature of all beings, born from the wisdom of the three vajras, O Vajraketana, HŪṂ-syllable, destroyer of the afflictions, homage be to you! 5.15
Homage to you, O foremost of all Buddhas, whose body is indivisible like the three vajras;
born from the selflessness of phenomena, the nectar of gnosis—homage be to you! (5.16)
O mass of omniscient wisdom, purifier of the nine wheels, great knowledge, great splendor, great hero—homage be to you! 5.17
O Great Jewel, O mighty-armed one, O Great Festival, O one of great strength!
O Destroyer of Māra, O Great Hero, O Lord of Heroes, homage be to you! 5.18
O Lord, you are the creator of the origin, maintenance, and destruction of the world;
O you who are the singular, most wonderful nature of both existence and non-existence, homage be to you! 5.19

Homage to you, who are to be known through wisdom; homage to you, the one who sets in motion the path to what is to be known. O Lord of the World, homage be to you; O Lotus-born One, homage, homage! 5.20
Having thus formally entreated the Lord with this king of hymns according to the ritual rules,
one should speak sweet words that desire the welfare of all sentient beings.
[She who is] desirous of my welfare; by the grace of your feet, O benefactor, I have come to know the unsurpassed practice.
Now, O Lord, bestow your grace through the jewel of consecration.
O Lord, just as that which is called the secret reality was shown by the glorious Mahāsukha to the glorious Dharmavajrin, so likewise, be gracious to me.
O Lord, deliver me from this hell, the abode of all sufferings;
show compassion to one who is protectorless, you who cut through every sorrow. 5.24
"O Lord, apart from your lotus feet, I have no other refuge;
therefore, be gracious, O foremost of Buddhas, hero of the world, great sage! (5.25)
Having thus heard this wondrous, divine, and supreme rite of entreaty,
the glorious Guru, an ocean of virtues, gave rise to compassion for the disciple.
Having become serene of face, compassionate, and joyful, he should cause [the disciple] to hear the divine commitments, which are more secret than the secret and supreme. 5.27.
"You must kill living beings, my son, and you must speak false words; you must accept what has not been given—this, in brief, is the rule. (5.28)
And every day, you must perform the practice of the supreme Mahāmudrā;
furthermore, you must observe the fourfold commitments (samaya) of Rudra.
Having thus made them hear the auspicious pledges that bestow all accomplishments,
the preceptor, moved by compassion, then becomes joined with the mudrās.
Through the union of the lotus and the vajra, the tradition is established;
having brought about the yoga of the deity, it is established exactly as it is. (5.31)
Having diligently grasped Padmasambhava with the speech-vajra, [and] having brought about the tradition...
The supreme preceptor [should prepare] a mixture of red and white [substances] for the purpose of worship.
Having added human semen together with feces, vajra-water,
and so forth, he then summons the disciple who has been empowered by all the Buddhas. (5.33)
Endowed with his own mudrā, he should cause him to receive the pledge (samaya), which is the abode of all siddhis and qualities, by means of the path of the Buddha’s empowerment. 5.34
Thus, according to the ritual procedure of the pledge, the knower of reality [should bestow] his own mudrā upon the vajra-disciple, together with the divine pledges enjoined therein. (5.35)
She has a beautiful face and large eyes, is always delighted in the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), is as pure as Māmakī, joyful, and has cast off her garments. (5.36)
Having properly worshipped him as he stands within the lotus of the mudrā,
one should honor the disciple with every ritual service, as if he were a second Vajradhara.
With auspicious and most excellent sounds, with various musical instruments and melodies,
with fans, banners, umbrellas, and other objects of worship, and with garlands, sandalwood paste, and the like.
Having established [the disciple] firmly and evenly with the jewel of the mudrā-consecration,
one should perform the consecration of the triple world for the disciple, who has joined his palms at the nails.
Then he should grant him the authorization prescribed by the tantra:
"Set in motion the vajra of the directions and the wheel of Dharma according to your wish."
Within the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
perform the teaching issued from the mouth of the supreme Buddha Vajrasattva.

Having thus firmly bestowed the well-guarded tradition upon the disciple, [he should grant] the consecration of the jewel-seal (mudrāratnābhiṣeka) and especially the authorization (anujñā). || 5.42 ||
And having spoken thus, O foremost of beings, you who have made a firm resolve through your own autonomy,
teach the instruction for the bodhisattvas that arises from the sequence of vajra-gnosis.
Consecrated by this method, the practitioner of firm resolve,
having exerted effort in the cultivation of reality, attains the unsurpassed state. (5.44)
The supreme Vajrasattva, having resolved upon perfect enlightenment, shall accomplish it through the yoga of the lineage succession, free from all dualities. (5.45)

Those whose minds are certain regarding the reality of the sequence of the tradition meditate upon the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, who bestows the accomplishment of all aims, their hearts gladdened by divine qualities of sensual pleasure. 5.46
Those men who abide in the *Śrīguhyasiddhi* achieve success in this very life;
endowed with the divine means (*divyopāya*), they go to the supreme, ineffable state.
Thus, all that has been understood through wisdom is established according to reasoning,
as set forth in the path of oral tradition through the sequence of the Śrīsamāja.
Then, abiding in self-will and striving for divine accomplishment,
one established in the secret accomplishment should practice among all castes.
Or else, joined with the mudrā and endowed with the five qualities of sensual pleasure—such as divine laughter, dance, and so forth, which bring about the exaltation of the mind. (5.49)
Or, intent upon the secret accomplishment, one should realize the supreme state,
liberated from all dualities and nourished by supreme bliss.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Initiation of the Great Seal for the Practitioner," in the *Śrī Guhyasiddhi*, extracted from the *Śrī Paramārthas tryakṣaratantra-sadbhāva*.
Chapter Six.
Therefore, I shall fully proclaim that secret practice which brings about auspiciousness, the mother of all Buddhas, and the destroyer of the enemy of distraction. (1)
Having cast off the spreading of the feet—that is, having abandoned the basket of saṃsāra—one whose mind is perpetually liberated should accomplish the command of Vajrasattva. (2)
Having diligently abandoned remorse, sloth, torpor, and the like, otherwise there would be no accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of eons. (3)
Having prostrated with one's entire being before the Lord, the Vajra-Teacher, one should practice the secret accomplishment through the form of the indivisible three vajras. (4)
Having made [the mind] signless and free from appearance, and joined with the means of one's own body, one should diligently meditate upon Vajrasattva, the supreme bliss. (5)

Having meditated thus with diligence upon his own body as auspiciously composed of all vajras, the mantra-practitioner [realizes] it to be, in its true nature, impenetrable even by the wielders of the vajra.
Filled with supreme bliss, he should observe the divine secret vow, illuminated by various modes of conduct and endowed with divine means.
Born from the womb of conceptual construction, that which is despised in the worlds through various practices and the like—
having fully assumed those very states of being, the practitioner should observe the secret vow. (8)
Just as the conduct known as "Secret" is established in the *Śrīsamāja*,
those who are fit for the practice indeed have the purpose of consuming excrement, urine, and food.
And by other divine observances, especially lamps and the like, as well as by various empowerments of mudrās and principles (tattvas) enjoined in the tantras. || 10 ||
Having spoken thus with these auspicious vajra-words by means of the mind-vajra,
I shall now explain with diligence that unsurpassed secret conduct. (11)
I shall explain in detail that which was concealed by the Mind-Vajra, for the benefit of the best of practitioners who desire the fruit of Buddhahood. (12)
Assuming the form of a madman, remaining silent and composed, with his self absorbed in the yoga of his own tutelary deity, he should wander about like a *piśāca*. 13.
The foremost of Vajrasattvas, having exerted himself repeatedly, should constantly meditate, being devoted to contemplation, upon the self as known through reasoning. (14)
One should wander through the villages and cities, in the grounds of the parks,
at crossroads, in cremation grounds, and likewise in temples.
And especially in the mountain fastness, having fashioned a crown from the remains of offerings,
he shall cause supreme happiness for the women in their dwellings.
But on Ajavīthi, one should resort to effortless music, crowded with dancers and celestial musicians, and provided with lamps fed by milk. (17)

In some places laughing, in some places talking, in some places he should cause songs to be sung; in some places dancing, in some places snapping his fingers, and in some places making various sounds. (18)
Everything should be done very gradually so that no weariness arises;
for when weariness has arisen, Buddhahood is never accomplished. (19)
One who has transcended worldly conduct should practice all the [esoteric] classes;
he should perform every gathering in the assembly and be intent upon that which is near the milk.
One should not cultivate excessive greed for things such as the nectar of immortality and so forth, even within the context of the *samaya* and other practices;
rather, one should practice only a very small amount for the sake of generating the sense of "I" (*ahaṅkāra*). 21.
Just as the consciousness of one whose mind is in supreme bliss does not become deluded,
so too must the practitioner perform all actions preceded by the observance of the pledges (*samaya*). || 22 ||
One should practice reality in such a way that the mind does not wither due to the sounds of dancing and singing,
until it has reached direct perception. (23)
He was solely devoted to the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and had resolved that they were his food;
he was anointed by Vairocana and adorned with the observance of a madman (unmattavrata).
All those signs belonging to the intoxicated state must always be performed according to the prescribed rule by the mantra-practitioner during the secret practices. (25)
One should always consume with effort, according to the prescribed rite, the lamp produced from the limbs of all living beings, for the sake of attaining divine perfection.
One should always worship oneself with substances such as feces and urine, mixed with flies and vomit, and infused with the five lamps.
Having generated merely as a conventional reality the glorious Mahāsukha-vajrin, who is without intrinsic nature and supremely peaceful, one should meditate upon the supreme state. (28)

Having meditated upon him in such a manner, the practitioner, intent on the realization of his own body, should perform all remaining duties, such as the cultivation of disgust and so forth, without hesitation. (29)
Taking hold of a beautiful flower endowed with the thought of awakening (bodhicitta),
one should grasp it and worship the Great Bliss with that Vajra of Speech.
The practitioner of mantra should constantly consume the lamp-like essence produced from humans— namely elephants, horses, donkeys, cows, and camels— but he should not consume ordinary food.
Whoever practices constantly with this yoga of reality will attain accomplishment; of this there is no doubt, according to the words of Padma and Vajra. (32)
A practitioner of the vow should not carry an alms-bowl for the purpose of wandering about seeking food;
rather, he eats from whatever he has gathered, such as a rag from the street or a discarded garment. (33)
He should wander for alms in that very place and eat while exerting himself;
having eaten there, being satisfied, he should discard it right there.
Then he should wear a loincloth, even if it is torn and tattered;
or else, having become naked, he may wander about as he pleases. (35)
One should not take possession of even an object as small as a sesame seed;
from possession arises suffering, and from suffering comes the delusion of the mind. (36)
Through delusion the mind dissolves; from that dissolution comes failure, and otherwise, success.
From the absence of success comes saṃsāra, and from saṃsāra one goes to hell. || 37 ||
For a duration measured in eons, one is tormented by the afflictions of suffering in hell;
thereafter, one is born dejected, with a wretched countenance, and as a servant to others. (38)
One does not obtain another birth that is distinguished and esteemed as a spiritual attainment;
thus, in the secret practice, one should contemplate the self within the self.
Endowed with divine means, pure, and uniform throughout the three realms,
one should then roam like a lion, established in the secret siddhi.
Assuming the garb of a madman and divesting himself of all formal appearances,
he should not even pay homage to the Goddess in the form of wood, stone, or clay.
One should indeed perform worship and pay homage to this very body of the Guru;
one should not construct stupas made of stone or clay, nor should one find delight in books.
One should not construct mandalas even in a dream, nor should one form mudrās with the hands; one should certainly not perform prostrations to those who abide on the path of the three vehicles. (43)
Even in a dream,
how could there be union with the Buddhas for others who merely bear the outward marks?
And one whose mind is intent on meditative cultivation should not engage in verbal disputes. || 44 ||
A lapse of the commitment arises through the mind; from that lapse, the mind becomes distracted.
One who knows reality should always avoid, in accordance with reality, the preliminary applications and so forth. (45)
One should not perform [any rite] other than by maintaining the ego-identification with Vajrasattva; and those established in the secret reality do not perceive [ordinary] ritual application. 46.
And the application [is as follows]:
"As long as that is being scrutinized through the application of the state of selflessness, for one who abides in the state of the lack of intrinsic nature and is endowed with divine means. (47)
Whatever has been enjoined by the ritual manual is accomplished through the immutable [state]; by the power of the yoga of meditative cultivation, it manifests of its own accord. (48)
All that, whatever constitutes the signs of accomplishment, occurs in a mere instant; one need not construct a mandala at all, for the binding consists simply in the forming of the mudrās. 49.
The practitioner of mantra should not recite the mantra if it creates an obstacle to meditative cultivation;
the body is said to be the mandala, and wisdom is celebrated as the mudrā. (50)
The minister, whose essence is the venerable Vajrasattva, should perform prostration and service;
the wise one should practice all this internally and abandon everything external. (51)
For the mantra-practitioner who has been consecrated in the secret conduct, who is free from conceptual construction,
through enthusiasm, union with reality, and the observance of the commitments (samayas), || 52 ||
Through association with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), through the cultivation of wisdom and skillful means,
and through the practice of dance, song, and so forth, as well as the miraculous manifestations of the lotus and vajra. || 53 ||
With offerings of spirits and lamps, with extensive arrays of perfumes and garlands, and with the sounds of lutes and drums, resounded by the noise of muraja drums. || 54 ||
Through hundreds of prostrations and the delights of celestial maidens, Vajrasattva is accomplished.
With these divine substances, either with devotion or through the cultivation of meditative concentration. || 55 ||
Vajrasattva is indeed accomplished; there is no need for deliberation here, because through the union of the vajra and the lotus, he exists in the form of supreme bliss. 56.
Through the relinquishing of the thought of awakening, one should enter into the consumption of what has been prescribed;
likewise for one who is constantly passionate, diligent, and longing for the bliss of women. 57.
"By means of emission, one should enter;
Vajrasattva is said to be accomplished. What more than this? Always becoming free from shame, one should be intent upon the conduct of the *samaya*. (58)
Wearing the garb of a madman, observing silence, and occasionally dwelling in cremation grounds, one should meditate on Vajrasattva together with his multitude of mudrās. 59.
...the abode;
...the multitude;
...endowed with.
Adorned with various ornaments such as Māmakī, Locanā, and the others, one should meditate there upon all [the deities] through their union with the Vajra of the Space-element (khadhātu). 60.
With the extensive radiations of the light of gnosis in the form of the three faces,
one should perform the withdrawal of the Buddhas who possess the nature of gnosis.
Through the application of the two organs and by means of the instructions on the sequence of one's own nature,
the jewel of the mind becomes firm by this yoga of meditation.
Established in the awakening of the Buddhas, they perform consecration;
having become thus and being firmly settled, one who is devoted to meditation should practice it. 63.
As long as the mind of the wise one remains composed and concentrated, he should remain so;
but once weary, he may wander about afterwards, acting according to his inclination. (64)
With eyes opened wide by the fear of awakening to vast enlightenment, one should meditate;
sometimes laughing, sometimes talking, sometimes standing, and sometimes performing a dance.
Just as no weariness arises for one whose mind is attached to cultivation,
so it is for the mantra-practitioner who is endowed with meditative concentration and free from conceptual construction. 66.
Abandoning the limitation of time, the unsurpassed state is accomplished;
one should daily perform the divine observances arising from the five families.
One should worship firmly with other special pledges as well, with eyes wide open and always possessing the disposition of a Sugata. (68)
Having directed the mind toward perfect enlightenment, one should cultivate the ocean of gnosis, being devoted to the jewel of conduct and possessing faith in the Vajrayāna. (69)
One who desires the state of a Sugata should never perform an unwholesome act in the mind;
one should desire every woman arisen within the three realms.
One should worship even a woman of low birth or one who is deformed, through the yoga of reality,
as she is born from Vairocana and produced from the limbs of all living beings. (6.71)
One desiring accomplishment should consume a living being through the yoga of reality, by means of feces, vajra-water, seeds, and so forth, which arise from within the nostrils. (6.72)
The practitioner of mantra should constantly worship within his own body through the meditations on the vajras;
he should always observe the commitments (samayas) arisen from the three realms. 6.73
Through the application of the jewel of reality, it is accomplished in no other way.
What is the use of saying much more here? Whatever may be perceived [is so through this]. (6.74)
All that should be viewed through the yoga of reality, as known by reasoning;
for everything indeed must be performed exactly as it is stated in the *Vajrasādhana*. (6.75)
Through the application of wisdom and means, there is the divine service of the commitments;
by performing it in this way, the mantra-practitioner truly [engages] in the secret conducts according to reality. (6.76)
Success is attained very quickly; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
The practitioner of mantra should constantly worship himself, being intent upon the ultimate reality.
Endowed with divine means, possessing a body inseparable from the three principles (tritatva),
and preceded by auspiciousness— this entire triple world is pure. (6.78)

Having thus diligently investigated that which is characterized by the aggregates, elements, and so forth— [which is] covered by the net of ignorance for those who follow the play of dreams, [and is] inseparable from the three principles (tritattva)— [one should realize it]. (6.79)
One should cultivate the signless and the appearance-less by means of the method;
having thus understood this, those who know the ritual should have their minds established in reality. 6.80
He should observe all the rules of conduct while subsisting on whatever he happens to obtain, through invitations from merchants, Brahmins, and Śūdras for specific purposes and the like. (6.81)
Once they have become satiated, whatever skull-bowl has been cast outside should be taken and eaten there like a dog; this is the desired, though loathsome, practice. (6.82)
