Through the yoga of the reality of meditative cultivation, it is not accomplished otherwise;
the conduct of all castes is somewhat like the behavior of a madman. (6.83)
It was surrounded on all sides by children making clapping sounds,
and it was endowed with hundreds of divine dances and songs accompanied by the rhythmic steps of the vajra-dance.
Emitting the sounds of songs and indistinct vajra-songs, one should cause others to perform clearly whatever is well-known in the three realms. (6.85)
The *geya* is mixed with various sounds; one should wander about like a *piśāca*.
For by whatever means beings are bound through their fierce karma, [so it is]. (6.86)
By that very same means, however, when combined with the [proper] methods (*upāya*), they are liberated from the bondage of existence;
having attained the supreme, peaceful reality (*tattva*) which is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). (6.87)
Endowed with divine means, one should accomplish the supreme state—that reality which is all beings, devoid of the grasped and the grasper. (6.88)
Having pervaded it, the divine, all-pervading, supreme, and auspicious state remains.
Having meditated upon that constantly, conjoined with the means of one's own body, || 6.89 ||
Free from all conceptual constructions, he proceeds toward unsurpassed enlightenment;
wherever he may be established, in that divine place and state.
Even those of evil conduct succeed in attaining perfect awakening if they have made a firm resolve for it,
having taken recourse to the vow of the madman with their minds established in reality. (6.91)
Those of evil conduct,
with their minds [purified], attain success in this very life through the supreme play of secret conduct.
Or if he is unable to abandon his very extensive residence; || 6.92 ||
Then, having entered the house, one should secretly observe the commitments (samayas), whether it be the conduct taught in the *Śrī-Guhyasiddhi* or that which arises from virtuous qualities. 6.93.
But being solely devoted to worldly conduct so that no distinction arises, he becomes manifest at night, intent exclusively on the practice of milk. (6.94)
One who is solely devoted to worldly conduct should perform [the ritual] together with a trustworthy consort (mudrā) and not otherwise;
and every day one should perform the commitments (samaya) regarding feces, urine, and so forth. (6.95)
One who is devoted to the practice of the samaya attains the unsurpassed reality, provided they have a well-guarded companion and possess the most excellent knowledge of reality. (6.96)
Together with that very [consort], one should perform the commitments (samaya) and so forth as taught in the Tantra, using divine women, divine enjoyments, and likewise divine beds and seats. (6.97)
One who is endowed with knowledge and has exerted effort in cultivating the true nature of reality attains accomplishment;
even at home, one who is constantly devoted to the conduct of the observances (samaya) always achieves success. 6.98
But one who has fallen away from the conduct of the samaya is neither in the house nor in the practice;
such is the case for one endowed with samādhi and delighting in divine knowledge. (6.99)
Vajrasattva is indeed accomplished when impelled by this procedure; [so too are] all the practices that have been proclaimed in manifold ways. (6.100)
Practices such as those involving contradictory unions and so forth, which are preceded by loathing—
all these rites are for the purpose of attaining divine accomplishments (*divyasiddhi*). (6.101)
This is for one engaged in the secret conduct who knows reality, and not otherwise;
herein, the division of all [these matters] is intended for the sake of making them directly perceptible.

Adopting a form that is censured by worldly custom, such as the marks of a sectarian ascetic, [practicing] contrary observances and so forth is known as the "Secret Accomplishment" (guhyasiddhi). (6.103)
But he who makes his dwelling here must live in a place that is held in contempt; lacking developed power, he subsists on the proceeds of a monastery. (6.104)
He openly establishes conventions and the like for those of low birth, and with a mind attached to worldly things, he constructs sacrificial pits and pavilions. (6.105)
The sacrificial pit and the pavilion— whether established according to the ritual rules or otherwise— are declared to be destroyers of the teaching.
Alternatively, he who has been declared to possess the [auspicious] marks performs the means of accomplishment here. || 6.106 ||
He should perform his commitments at night or by day, well-concealed, so that he is not seen by others—by Śrāvakas of inferior birth. (6.107)
In this way, indeed, the counselor should act with great secrecy for the sake of his own success,
so that he is not oppressed by people and does not oppress people. (6.108)
Thus, in this matter, the counselor who desires the state of a Sugata must act; for he obstructs those who do not abandon the world.
As long as that which is established in the secret accomplishment has not arisen. || 6.109 ||
A practitioner should not wear the insignia as long as there is only some slight excellence;
however, once supreme excellence has arisen, he should then abandon the secret conduct.
Immediately thereafter, one should take up the divine vow of knowledge (*vidyāvrata*).

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Sequence of All Divisions of Secret Conduct for Purifying the Contemplation of the Equality of the Practitioner," in the *Śrīguhyasiddhi*, extracted from the *Paramārthasatyatryakṣaratantrasadbhāva*.
The Seventh Chapter: Having attained the supreme, divine, pure mudrā, which is the abode of all virtues, endowed with manifold forms, and free from sorrow and death; || 7.1 ||
A goddess, a nāginī, likewise a yakṣī, or an asurī, or a kinnarī;
one endowed with the form of a gandharvī, or perhaps a perfected yoginī. (7.2)
The yogin, having drawn forth these divine women, should worship them through the yoga of the reality of meditative cultivation, by means of the procedures involving the noose and the goad.
The diligent accomplishment of the divine [deities] is known as that very *samaya*;
once accomplished, they become servants and perform whatever is desired. (7.4)
And those [mudrās] never cause distraction of the mind at any time.
By means of the accomplished divine observances, the divine women possess great supernatural power.
Having attained great power and prosperity, free from urine and sweat,
they shall constantly enjoy celestial women who possess various forms and gait.
Always joined with them, the mantra-practitioner should roam like a lion in a secluded forest, free from all fear. (7.7)
If, however, he is unable to attract those divine women, [he should proceed as follows].

In order to attract celestial women,
for one who is not intent upon divine enjoyments, [this is for] the pacification of distraction and madness.

Furthermore, if divine [consorts] are unavailable, for the sake of accomplishing the goals of one's own success,
one should serve a human maiden who follows after all ritual activities.
Having thus formed the general mudrā in accordance with the tantra,
one whose mind is intent upon the supreme mudrā shall accomplish supreme enlightenment.
I shall now explain those common mudrās in their proper order, beginning with that of the lowest caste, by means of which spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) is attained. 7.13.
Whether she be an outcaste, a sister, a mother, a daughter, a dyer’s wife, or even one born of a despised family, another woman may be obtained for the sake of pleasures. (7.14)
Having especially made his daughter a follower of the tantra,
he should gradually perform the training of the child and so forth through all the ritual observances.

Having made those who delight in the jewel of the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*) skillful and indeed patient regarding the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the wise one should accomplish [the goal] according to the ritual procedure within her whose form consists of the indivisibility of the three vajras. (7.16)
Established there, one should begin the worship as prescribed and enjoined by the tantra,
with offerings of milk-lamps, perfumes, garlands, and other elaborate provisions.
Having smeared his divine form with ashes and adorned it with a crown of matted locks,
the mantra-practitioner should likewise especially fashion his own image.
Clad in a tiger-skin garment and adorned with various ornaments,
he took up a vajra-khaṭvāṅga together with a skull-cup and a hand-drum.
Adorned with fragments of bone on his ear, neck, and arm,
he holds a human skull in his left hand and likewise a hand-drum (ḍamaruka) in his right.
Having assumed the form of the *Ṛgveda* and likewise that of the mudrā of oneself,
one should personally become the bearer of the supreme vajra by means of Māmakī, Locanā, and the others. (7.21)
One should observe the divine vow of knowledge according to the sequence of rites prescribed in the Kalpa;
having made a firm resolve free from dualities, one attains perfection in this very life.

The wise one, firm in his resolve for Buddhahood, should observe the vow of knowledge (vidyāvrata); by means of the commitments (samaya) taught in the tantra, he will certainly attain accomplishment in this very life. (8.16)
In mountains, at the edge of the ocean, in a kingdom free from defects,
in regions of great forests, in cities, and in ancient caves.
In secluded places, especially those filled with great trees and creepers, agitated by fruit-bearing trees surrounded by clear water.

Delighting in the Vajrayāna and always possessing the disposition of a Sugata, having practiced all [these qualities] without exception, he is generous, heroic, and likewise skillful. (8.22)

She is endowed with the profound nature of reality, follows the desires of the practitioner,

Delighting in the thought of awakening, skillful and well-guarded in the Vajra practice, one should treat a brother with affection as one would a son, and likewise as one would a father. (8.25)
Filled with an excess of affection, she constantly gazes upon the practitioner;

Free from envy, well-disposed, and obedient to the instructions of the practitioner—Gaurī is slender, beautiful, and adorned with virtues and good character. (8.27)

she may be twelve years old from birth, or sixteen years old.
Devoted to the knowledge of reality, she was graced by a beautiful dark complexion;
she was complete in all her limbs, with hair that was curly at the ends and beautifully matted.
Content with her sweet voice and possessing wide, auspicious eyes—
having obtained such a maiden with effort for the sake of achieving success.
Then the vow of knowledge (vidyāvrata) should be performed as previously stated and enjoined in the ritual manual (kalpa).
Having grasped that with diligence, one should accomplish the supreme state. 8.31 ||
Having worshipped with one's own vajra, one should emit the thought of awakening (bodhicitta);
then, having meditated upon the body-vajra, one should take it up with the speech-vajra. || 8.32 ||

One should worship the white [semen], arisen from his [the practitioner's] private parts, as the Mind-Vajra; having worshipped it with devotion according to the sequence of rites arising from sexual union. (8.33)
Through the yoga of the reality of cultivation, one should practice Cundā or Māmakī as appropriate;
indeed, everything must be performed by means of the meditative visualizations of the initial yoga. (8.34)
One should engage in the service of divine women, especially in accordance with the *samayas*;
having placed the *liṅga* in the *bhaga*, one must not emit the *bodhicitta*.
Having agitated that bliss and filled the mind, the mantra practitioner should meditate until he performs the emission of the bodhicitta. (8.36)
For that long, one attains an uninterrupted, indescribable bliss born of joy;
through that very form of bliss, one is united with supreme Śiva. (8.37)
One should constantly cultivate the self; one will attain accomplishment, of this there is no doubt, even if this bodhicitta—the treasury of all accomplishments—has fallen away. (8.38)
When the aggregate of consciousness has arisen, how can there be blameless accomplishment?
For one must agitate that seat, which is intensely overflowing with the pure bodhicitta. (8.39)
Embracing the mudrā in reality, one should kiss her again and again;
having kissed that Vidyā through the meditations on the Mahāmudrā. (8.40)
With her pair of eyes wide open and her lower lip slightly quivering,
she was divine with her two stainless thighs, her eyes somewhat half-closed like buds.
Devoted to the cultivation focused on that [truth], having exerted effort in the Vajrayāna, her mind was constantly directed toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and likewise the Saṅgha. (8.42)
Having honored that Saṅgha especially with repeated offerings of milk, according to the yoga of the reality of meditative cultivation, one should [offer] the mudrā to the Vajrin. (8.43)
Subsequently, with honors such as perfumes and garlands, and with those other captivating things—
fish, meat, spirits, and the like— which cause the mind to become exalted; (8.44)
Having thus worshipped with diligence, one intent upon reality should meditate;
impelled by that ritual procedure, one becomes perfected as the very self of Vajrasattva. (8.45)
Having obtained the nectar of flowers, endowed with the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), and possessing the divine splendor of the space-element, one should worship the Vajrin with that. 8.46.
Thus, accomplishment is swiftly attained through the practice and cultivation of the commitments;
however, for one whose mind harbors hatred toward the commitments, no accomplishment is proclaimed by the Jinas.
Having understood the yoga of the deity and the observance of the pledges, and having meditated upon that with effort, one attains accomplishment; there is no doubt in this matter. || 8.48 ||
In the aforementioned places, the wise man who has fulfilled the vow of knowledge,
having become cleansed of all impurity, shall fly up together with that knowledge.
In this matter, there is neither a mandatory injunction nor a prohibition regarding whether it be in a village or even a city;
one should practice the vow of knowledge in whatever place is agreeable to the mind. (8.50)
That which was taught as the means of accomplishment in the *Śrī-samāja* tantra is clearly set forth there, together with the secret conduct and endowed with the observance of the vidyā. (8.51)
By one who is joined with the practice of the pledge (samaya) and who meditates constantly, the accomplishment spoken from the mouth of Vajrasattva occurs swiftly. (8.52)
[The word *bhāvitena* is the emendation of the editor; it was previously *bhāvatena*.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Extraction of the Assembly," in the *Śrīguhyasiddhi*, which is extracted from the *Paramārthatrikṣaratantrasadbhāva*.
Those who do not know the means [to overcome danger] regarding fire, water, poison, and so forth...
They dissolve, they burn, they die; there is no doubt in this. || 9.1 ||
Likewise, in the tantra known as the *Samāja*, those who are devoid of skillful means and practice what is contrary [to the teachings] fall away, being difficult to save. (9.2)
But those beings who, among the traditions, strive for the knowledge of reality therein, they quickly extend [the lineage], being devoted to the Śrīsamāja. 9.3.
The vow of secret conduct and the mudrā that have been described at length—
all this is called conceptual construction and consists solely of mere mental cultivation. (9.4)
Whatever has been taught in this [work] in an extensive form according to the dispositions of all sentient beings,
that is accomplished by one who is endowed with knowledge and established in meditative cultivations. (9.5)
Having abandoned everything here— the extensive elaborations arising from conceptual construction— the wise one should constantly and with effort meditate upon Mahāmudrā. (9.6)
One who practices repeatedly and is free from all pairs of opposites attains perfection before long, just as Padmavajra did.
And among all commitments, the worship of the guru is supreme;
likewise, the Śrīsamāja and other [tantras] are the jewel-casket of the Buddhas.
Whether it be unmanifest and to be grasped with effort, or abiding within all sentient beings, it is non-conceptual and free from affliction through the distinctions of body, speech, and mind. (9.9)
It is traditionally taught that the bodhicitta is pure and devoid of intrinsic nature;
its attainment occurs swiftly through the grace of the guru’s feet. (9.10)
There is nothing superior to the teacher, who is like a jewel within the three realms.
Through faith in him, the wise attain manifold accomplishments. (9.11)
The teacher should practice that conduct which was proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Speaker of Reality, as being equal and non-dual; otherwise, one will certainly not attain accomplishment. 9.12

Having adorned her with garments, ornaments, enjoyments, and so forth, one should offer her as one's own mudrā for the sake of worshipping the guru and for the attainment of the siddhi of the Buddhas. (9.13)
Success as enjoined in the Tantra arises from the offering of one's own mudrā; otherwise, there is no success at all through external observances (samaya) as enjoined. 9.14
This indeed is the most supreme commitment (*samaya*) within the *Tantrasadbhāva*, spoken by the illustrious Vajranātha for the benefit of practitioners. 9.15.
For all commitments (*samaya*), the offering of one's own mudrā is supreme; otherwise, through commitments that are merely external in form, success is never attained. 9.16
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship the Guru with devotion through the offering of one's own mudrās, lotuses, and the like, as well as with songs arising from his throat. 9.17
With the sounds of frogs and the music of cymbals, with the dancing of vajra-possession, with the tasting of the fruits of the Vidyādharas, and with the festivals of slight embraces. (9.18)
Prompted by the Tantra, he [offered] various kinds of cooked foods—such as *pūpikās*, *kuśukas*, and *dalluras*—along with divine drinks like *śīdhu* and fish, and other diverse items. 9.19.
From that, however, the supreme perfection arises in the offering of one's own seal;
otherwise, for one who does not follow this method, there will be no perfection at all.
Those who, by this method, practice devotion toward the Vajra-Teacher through the path permeated by reality, [attain] the stainlessness of the non-differentiation of the three vajras. (9.21)
In this regard, those beings obtain the well-guarded oral transmission,
which bestows all siddhis and is divine, once the Guru-Vajrī is satisfied. (9.22)

Thus firmly established by the divine commitments (samaya) declared in the tantras, they swiftly bestow the oral tradition (sampradāya) which is supreme in the ritual activity of the Vajrācārya. (9.23)
Having clearly understood the reality according to this method and in accordance with the scriptures, one attains Buddhahood, which is further nourished by the state of devotion. (9.24)
Having first paid homage to the Guru with devotion at the time of worship, one should do so with diligence according to the tradition.
Afterwards, one should meditate upon that supreme mind, which is auspicious and bestows the siddhi of a Buddha. || 9.25 ||
Those who are intent on reviling their guru, especially those who revile the holders of the Vajra, and those who cause harm to the Three Jewels— one should diligently slay them. (9.26)
[They are] distinguished from the holders of the vajra. Those who do not know the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) of the Buddhas, which is like the sky...
Having heard this supreme method, those beings will not cross over.
Those beings who revile the Vajrayāna and possess inferior inclinations will go to the states of woe for as many as a hundred eons.
Those of inferior inclinations,
though they have crossed over the miserable states (apāya) by means of intense falls within cyclic existence (saṃsāra),
are cast down due to their evil deeds, arising from suffering and poverty. (9.29)
Those who, having taken up the outward signs of a follower of the Sugata, show no respect for the Buddha, the Dharma, and likewise the Saṅgha, shall go to the Avīci hell. (9.30)
But those who, endowed with devotion, shall cultivate the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
being shaken free from all evils, they shall become leaders.
Endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, they will cause beings to cross over from the terrible ocean of saṃsāra toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment.
Before long, they will become teachers of the entire world,
[establishing] the unsurpassed state within the awakening of a Buddha regarding the supreme dharmas. (9.33)
For the sake of sentient beings blinded by the darkness of ignorance, they will produce the light of knowledge from the perspective of ultimate reality, like a lamp in the dark. (9.34)
Those who constantly and with devotion remember the two lotus feet of the sole Lord of Great Bliss, which cut through all sins. (9.35)
By his power alone, those beings will before long become like the Lotus-Bearer, the Lord of the World, a treasury of all accomplishments. (9.36)
Whatever sādhana of Śrī Vajrasattva has been composed by me through secret practice, with a pure mind firmly drawn in by the goad of devotion; (9.37)
This is indeed auspicious; what more auspicious than the auspicious could be said?
If this was not a jest, nor was it a true friend, may the teachers forgive me for that. 9.38.

Whatever has not been understood by me here, which I have attempted to explain in accordance with the tantras, all that should be forgiven by the Noble Ones, as one would forgive one's own child. (9.39)
Composed by Padmavajra, who subsists on the lotus feet of the Lord of Great Bliss, out of compassion for all sentient beings. 9.40.
Known by the name Śrī Guhyasiddhi, it is the most excellent among all accomplishments;
it should be practiced with diligent effort by practitioners who desire liberation. 9.41
By this [practice], a wise man shall attain complete perfection in this very life, provided that he practices the secret accomplishment as prescribed according to the ritual. (9.42)
May all that [be] auspicious for the venerable Great Master (śrīmahācāryapāda);
by which secret practice, accompanied by all sentient beings, there may be accomplishment. 9.43 ||

All mental constructions have been shaken off by those who are difficult for sense-objects to overcome, even though their minds were once attached; they are now peaceful and bring about the attainment of Buddhahood.
In an instant, one falls into saṃsāra, which is afflicted by the five states [of affliction]:
torpor and drowsiness, remorse, restlessness, and doubt. (9.45)
In the world of saṃsāra, which is afflicted by calamities; [emendation from *saṃsāra* in MS to *saṃsāre* as per the edition]; [emendation from *upadrutam* in MS to *upadrute* as per the edition];
[emendation from *-siddhā-* in MS to *-middhyā-* as per the edition].
One will not attain Buddhahood for a Bodhisattva due to the five obscurations;
having abandoned those five, one becomes certain of attaining Buddhahood. (9.46)
One attains accomplishment in this very life through the playful observance of the madman’s vow.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Teaching on the Worship of the Ultimate Master," in the *Śrīguhyasiddhi*, extracted from the true essence of the *Akṣaratantra* concerning the ultimate reality.
Thus ends the Guhyasiddhi, which incites one toward the true essence of all tantras.
